clue.text: Flying jet that's extremely huge, I've right to be nervous

indicators.note: flying here means sent all over the place, so the letters gathered before it are scattered and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, minus the apostrophe

indicators.note: extremely points to the extreme letters, the first and last, of huge

parts.note: taken as written, minus the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone aboard an enormous jet plane feels entitled to be scared of flying.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram pool is JET, THATS, HE (the outer letters of 'huge'), IVE and R, fourteen letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: having the jitters is being nervous or jumpy, so the phrase replaces 'to be nervous' directly.

clue.text: Dismiss teacher, one caught out misbehaving? She may want to

indicators.note: misbehaving means behaving wrongly, so the remaining letters are put in a disordered arrangement
out says the letters for one and caught are removed from the words dismiss teacher

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A troublemaking pupil caught misbehaving makes someone want to get rid of a teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: Take I and C out of DISMISSTEACHER and rearrange what is left. The definition leans on the start of the clue: she may want to dismiss a teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: A school's female head is the person with the authority to fire a member of staff, so she may wish to do the dismissing.

clue.text: Old film star from Depression any number can love

parts.note: a vale is a valley, a depression in the land
N stands for any number in algebra
a tin is a can
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: A silent-era idol is drawn from the Depression, a figure anyone could fall for.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudolph Valentino was a silent-film heartthrob of the 1920s, a star of a bygone era.

clue.text: Melody Maker originally penned by old solver?

indicators.note: penned by means enclosed by, so the letter goes inside the old word for you

parts.note: the solver is addressed as you, and thee is the old form of you

indicators.note: originally points to the first letter of Maker

explanation.surface: Mentions the music paper Melody Maker, as if its founder's writing were done by an elderly puzzler.
explanation.walkthrough: Melody Maker was a British weekly music paper; here the two words are split, Melody the definition and Maker supplying its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is a tune or musical subject, which is what a melody is.

clue.text: Former partner's on box, maybe pocketing millions? That's excessive

indicators.note: on means placed next to, joining the two parts end to end

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse or partner

indicators.note: pocketing means taking into a pocket, so the letter for millions goes inside the tree

parts.note: box is an example of a tree, hence the maybe

explanation.surface: An ex-partner seen on television, perhaps raking in millions, is going too far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like the television; with 'maybe' it is the box tree, an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Extreme and excessive are synonyms, both describing something going far beyond what is reasonable.

clue.text: Klingsor's favourite nurse regularly provides motivation

parts.note: Klingsor is the setter, so Klingsor's is I'm
a pet is a favourite

indicators.note: regularly picks every other letter of nurse

explanation.surface: The setter's beloved nurse is what keeps them going.
explanation.definitionFit: Impetus is the driving force or momentum behind an action, so it is a synonym of motivation.

clue.text: Explain why I won't reach Euston on time? Not I

indicators.note: not here means without, so the letter I is taken away from the phrase

parts.words: why I won't reach Euston on time
parts.note: the excuse for missing an arrival at a London station is that the train's late

explanation.surface: A traveller explains why they will arrive late at Euston, a London railway terminus.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I from TRAINSLATE. 'Not I' looks like an aside from the speaker but is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To translate can mean to interpret or put into plainer terms, so it is a synonym of explain.

clue.text: In Don Juan's embrace, girl's beginning to blush

indicators.note: in, paired with embrace, says one piece sits inside the other
an embrace encloses, so the rake's word wraps around the letter

parts.note: Don Juan is the archetypal rake, and a roue is a debauched man

indicators.note: beginning points to the first letter of girl's

explanation.surface: A girl in a seducer's arms starts to turn red.
explanation.walkthrough: Put G inside ROUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Rouge is red make-up applied to the cheeks, also called blusher, so it is the noun blush in a cosmetic sense.

clue.text: Illness caused by food that's left a bit late?

indicators.note: a bit late says the letter for left arrives slightly further along in the word

parts.note: aliment is food or nourishment

explanation.surface: Someone falls sick from eating food that was left out too long.
explanation.walkthrough: In ALIMENT, move L one place later to get the answer. 'Left' looks like leftovers but is just L.
explanation.definitionFit: An ailment is a minor sickness or complaint, a synonym for illness.

clue.text: Capital German company invested in Leith?

indicators.note: invested in means put inside, so the company letters go into the first name

parts.note: Prue Leith is a British cookery writer and television judge
AG, Aktiengesellschaft, is the German term for a public company

explanation.surface: A German firm puts money into Leith, the Edinburgh port.
explanation.walkthrough: Leith looks like the port of Edinburgh; it is Prue Leith, the British cookery presenter, giving PRUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Prague is the capital city of the Czech Republic.

clue.text: Course tackling image building given by North European businessman

indicators.note: given by says the following letters are attached after what comes first
tackling means taking on or grappling with, so the course wraps around the public relations letters

parts.note: an entree is a course of a meal
PR, public relations, is the business of building an image
EUR is an abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A northern European trader is building his image through a training course.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrepreneur is someone who sets up businesses, so it is a kind of businessman.

clue.text: Filling that's nice — mm! — in pie snack?

indicators.note: printers' pie is type jumbled up, so letters in pie are scrambled

parts.note: to snack is to eat

explanation.surface: Someone praises the tasty filling of a pie they are snacking on.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange NICEMM to MINCEM, then add EAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Mincemeat, a mixture of dried fruit and spices, is what fills a mince pie.

clue.text: Radiance observed when one's lit up?

definitions.meaning: radiance is a bright glow or brilliance
a gleam is what appears on a surface once light falls on it

explanation.surface: A glow is noticed whenever someone is illuminated.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is cryptic: the glossy shine you see on something only shows when it is lit.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheen is a soft lustre or shine on a surface, so it is a synonym of radiance.

clue.text: It could be scoundrel taking in damsel heartlessly

definitions.text: It could be scoundrel taking in damsel heartlessly

indicators.note: taking in means enclosing, so the rascal's word wraps the letters

parts.note: a swine is a contemptible person, a scoundrel

indicators.note: heartlessly removes the inside of damsel, leaving its outer letters

explanation.surface: A cad cheating a young woman out of her money.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as a picture of a con: 'taking in' also means deceiving, done to a damsel without any heart.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone in is to deceive them, and a scoundrel heartlessly duping a young woman is a classic fraud.

clue.text: Drink leaves Mark full of energy — for workforce that's ideal

indicators.note: full of means containing, so the letters for drink, leaves and Mark hold the energy letter

parts.note: a dram is a small drink of spirits
E is the symbol for energy
tea is made from leaves

explanation.surface: A tipple and a cuppa leave Mark buzzing, ideal for staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb, as in departs; it is tea leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A dream team is a perfectly assembled group of people for a job, so an ideal workforce.

clue.text: Scruple restraining Queen's image-maker

indicators.note: restraining means holding in, so the abbreviation is split open around the queen

parts.note: scr. is the abbreviation for scruple, the old apothecaries' weight
Anne is the queen, Queen Anne of Britain; the 's is a link

explanation.surface: A qualm stops the monarch's photographer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scruple' reads as a moral qualm but is the apothecaries' weight, abbreviated scr.
explanation.definitionFit: A scanner produces pictures, such as medical scans or digital copies, so it makes images.

clue.text: Nobody of note, tiny person ultimately? Possibly

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter of person
possibly means in some possible version, so the letters may be put in another order

explanation.surface: Asks whether a small person might be a figure of no importance.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonentity is an unimportant person, so a nobody in the figurative sense.

clue.text: They give resistance to Tories violently?

definitions.text: They give resistance to Tories violently

parts.note: R is the symbol for electrical resistance

indicators.note: violently means with wild force, so the letters of Tories are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Protesters take on the Conservative Party with force.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a violent mob resisting the Tories, Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: People who take part in a violent public disturbance, resisting the government by force, are a mob of protesters.

clue.text: Fight and beat tough character

parts.note: to spar is to fight, as boxers do
to tan someone is to beat them

explanation.surface: A battler who fights and wins is a hard person.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spartan, after the austere warriors of ancient Sparta, is a hardy, self-disciplined person.

clue.text: Removal of corruption's unproductive in football tournament?

indicators.note: in places the unproductive word inside the tournament

parts.note: a cup is a knockout football competition
a lean period is unproductive

explanation.surface: Asks whether stamping out corruption in a football tournament brings no reward.
explanation.definitionFit: A clean-up is a purge of wrongdoing, so it is the removal of corruption.

clue.text: Lacy clothes fashionable with clubs? On reflection that's doubtful

indicators.note: on reflection means as in a mirror, so the whole assembly is turned backwards
clothes is used as a verb meaning covers, so lacy wraps around the fashionable letters

parts.note: in means fashionable
C is the card abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: Wonders whether lacy outfits are really in vogue at nightclubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' is a verb here, meaning covers, not the noun; 'On reflection' turns LACINYC around.
explanation.definitionFit: Cynical describes a sceptical outlook that distrusts others' motives, so it is a sense of doubtful.

clue.text: Resort's minute, for a start

parts.note: a spa is a resort, and with the 's it gives spas

explanation.surface: A holiday resort's tiny amount of something, at least to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute' reads as tiny but is M, and 'for a start' looks like a first-letter instruction; 'start' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A start can mean a sudden involuntary jerk, which is what a twitch or convulsion of the muscles is.

clue.text: A not half sad affair

indicators.note: not half removes half of the word for sad, keeping its first four letters

parts.note: mournful means sad

explanation.surface: A romance that is anything but gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' looks like the British slang for 'very', making a very sad affair; here it cuts MOURNFUL to MOUR.
explanation.definitionFit: An amour is a love affair, often a secret one, borrowed from the French word for love.

clue.text: Put crudely, can anyone bother?

indicators.note: put crudely means expressed in a rough way, so the letters are roughly rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks, bluntly, whether anybody can be bothered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bother' looks like a verb, ending the question; it is a noun meaning nuisance.
explanation.definitionFit: Annoyance and bother are synonyms as nouns, both meaning irritation or nuisance.

clue.text: Yen for maiden in island port

indicators.note: for means in place of, so the yen letter replaces the maiden letter

parts.note: Malta is a Mediterranean island
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
Y is the abbreviation for the Japanese currency yen

explanation.surface: Someone longs for a young woman living in a harbour town on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yen' reads as a longing, but it is the currency, Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Yalta is a Black Sea port in Crimea, scene of the 1945 Allied conference.

clue.text: Charlie's open secret

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet; the 's is a link
overt means open, not hidden

explanation.surface: Charlie's secret is an open one, known to all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open secret' reads as a set phrase, but the two words are wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Covert means hidden or concealed, a synonym of secret.

clue.text: Two names (the first abbreviated) for mineral

indicators.note: the first abbreviated says the first of the two words loses its last letter

parts.note: to call and to cite both mean to name

explanation.surface: A mineral bears a two-part name, the first part shortened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Names' reads as a noun; it is the verb, giving CALL and CITE, with CALL cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: Calcite is a common crystalline form of calcium carbonate, so it is an example of a mineral.

clue.text: Brief visit involves run then I'm at home, awfully weary

indicators.note: then says the next part follows on
involves means wraps up, so the visit holds the run, I'm and at home letters

parts.note: a call is a short visit
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
taken as written, minus the apostrophe
in means at home

indicators.note: awfully means badly done, so the letters of weary are disarranged

explanation.surface: A tired person describes a quick call that includes a run before getting home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' looks like an adjective, short; it is the noun, British slang for a lawyer. CALL holds RIMIN, then weary rearranges to AWYER.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a brief is a barrister or solicitor, especially one defending in court.
